To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Chlamydia‐infected patients mount mucosal antibody‐secreting cell (ASC) responses to the plasmid protein, pgp3; and that the ASCs are predominantly IgA in genital infection and in Gambian children, but are predominantly IgG in patients with extragenial complications of infection.

we have identified an important Chlamydia antigen, pgp3, which is a plasmid encoded protein and is highly conserved across all Chlamydia species, that we have shown that this antigen induces both mucosal (IgA) and systemic (IgG) antibody responses in patients with genital infection, that these antibody responses are highly specific to the chlamydia antigen (pgp3) and that we have also demonstrated that the antibody responses to pgp

(i) plasmid protein 3 is a promising antigen for serological diagnosis of genital chlamydiosis; (ii) the immune response to pgp3 is predominantly of the IgA isotype, and is localized at the site of infection; and (iii) the immune response is suppressed during severe disease, and is restored after antibiotic treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immune responses to the chlamydia plasmid protein, pgp3, and the potential use of this protein in the diagnosis and treatment of chlamydial disease.
the development of a new vaccine to protect women against the common sexually transmitted bacterial pathogen Chlamydia.
the characterization of the immune response in human and animal models of Chlamydia infection and its relationship to pathology and disease outcome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pgp3‐based ELISA is not a good test for chlamydial infections.
the immune response to pgp3 is complex, with the predominant response being IgA.
the pgp3‐based vaccine is not yet ready for human use.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pgp3 is a promising antigen for future studies of human chlamydial infections.
pgp3 is a promising candidate for a subunit vaccine against genital and ocular chlamydial infections.
the plasmid protein Pgp3 is a good candidate for a vaccine against genital Chlamydia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have demonstrated that the plasmid protein, pgp3, is an important target antigen for both humoral and cellular immunity in humans infected with C. trachomatis.
the plasmid protein PgP3 is an excellent target for vaccine development.

we found a very strong association between the presence of circulating pgp3‐ specific ASCs and the presence of chlamydiacervicitis, and that this association is not seen with the other chlamydia‐ specific antigens that we tested.
